entities.name: Assemblies of God
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Assemblies of God (AG), founded April 2-12, 1914 in Hot Springs, Arkansas at the Grand Opera House by approximately 300 ministers and laypeople responding to the Azusa Street Revival's Pentecostal awakening (1906-1909), is the world's largest Pentecostal denomination — with 69 million members globally in 400,000+ congregations across 240 countries, making it one of the largest Christian denominations in the world. The AG's rapid global growth through the 20th century is among the most remarkable institutional expansions in religious history.

The Azusa Street Revival (1906, Los Angeles, led by William Seymour) was the founding event of American Pentecostalism — the Holy Spirit 'baptism with fire' manifested in speaking in tongues (glossolalia) was interpreted as a new Pentecost. Ministers from Azusa scattered globally; the 1914 Hot Springs convocation created an institutional structure. The AG adopted Trinitarian Pentecostal theology (in contrast to 'Oneness' Pentecostals who reject the Trinity) in 1916.

Global AG growth has been most dramatic in Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, and Asia: Brazil's Assemblies of God (Assembleias de Deus, founded 1911 by Swedish missionaries Daniel Berg and Gunnar Vingren) is Brazil's largest Protestant denomination with 12+ million members; AG churches dominate Guatemalan, Salvadoran, and Honduran religious life. The AG ordained women from 1935; notable ministers include Oral Roberts (who founded Oral Roberts University) and Jimmy Swaggart (televangelist).

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Assemblies of God — growing from 300 ministers at a 1914 Arkansas opera house to 69 million members globally — is one of history's fastest institutional expansions, and its Pentecostal model (emotional worship, speaking in tongues, direct Holy Spirit experience) transformed global Christianity's dominant expression in the 20th century.
